newsitem.title: USA: Montgomery Ward files for bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: Montgomery Ward files for bankruptcy.

text.p: Montgomery Ward & Co., the 125-year-old department store chain, filed for bankruptcy protection Monday after talks with lenders aimed at rescuing the ailing retailer failed.

The 400-store chain had been negotiating desperately with lenders on a financing package involving fresh funding to pay vendors and obtain waivers on $1.4 billion in debt, but the negotiations collapsed.
"We have a realistic strategic business plan that will return Montgomery Ward to profitability," Montgomery Ward Chairman Roger Goddu said in a statement.

The company's Signature Group direct-marketing division was not a part of the filing, the company said. It said it was close to signing an agreement to sell the division to HFS Inc., a large hotel franchiser and owner of Avis car rental company, for an undisclosed sum.
The bankruptcy filing in Delaware caps a long struggle for the company, which posted a $249 million loss last year after earnings of $11 million in 1995.

The filing represents a major hit for General Electric Co.'s GE Capital Services division, which owns half of Montgomery Ward. GE said it wrote off in the second quarter its investment in Montgomery Ward's stock, which it acquired during a $3.8 billion leveraged buyout of Ward in 1988.

"We are convinced that Montgomery Ward's filing under Chapter 11 of the Bankruptcy Code is the best way for the company to conclude a quick and effective restructuring," Edward Stewart, executive vice president of GE Capital, said in a statement.

Montgomery Ward on Monday received a $1 billion facility from GE to help it pay for inventory during its bankruptcy reorganization. Despite its write-off, GE Capital said it "expects to announce strong double-digit earnings growth for the quarter.

Montgomery Ward already had borrowed millions from GE Capital this year to stay afloat. Still, it grew strapped for cash and recently stopped paying vendors late last month. In return, several suppliers stopped shipping merchandise.
"Inventory is like blood," said Barry Bryant of Rodman & Renshaw Inc. "If it doesn't flow, the patient dies."

Montgomery Ward had been seeking approval from banks and insurance companies of a package put together by GE Capital involving fresh funding and waivers on $1.4 billion in debt. But sources said the effort fell apart after at least one insurance company balked.
The sale of Signature to HFS Inc. was expected to raise about $1 billion, according to reports.

Under a proposal put together by GE, the company's lenders would have received about $600 million from the Signature sale, sources said. GE Capital would have injected a fresh $200 million in fresh financing and would have converted $265 million in unsecured funding to secured status.
Montgomery Ward said it was confident the company could rebound from its difficulties.

"Although a Chapter 11 bankruptcy filing was not our desired course of action, we believe that with the cooperation of our vendors and our associates, it will allow us to concentrate on implementing our merchandising strategy and emerge as a healthier contemporary retailer," Goddu said.

Last week, Ward said it would remodel four to six stores early next year to boost sales and attract its target customer, which it defined as between 30 and 55 years old and earning $25,000 to $50,000 a year. It also planned to focus on its core appliance and furniture businesses.
Montgomery Ward announced its filing after stock markets closed. Earlier Monday, GE stock rose 50 cents to $69.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
